cards.h: Feynman called it the one mystery
cards.b:
Richard Feynman said the double-slit experiment contains "the only mystery" of quantum mechanics. If you understand one experiment, make it this one. It needs no equations, only a screen with two slits.

It shows in one go why quantum objects cannot be thought of as ordinary balls or ordinary waves.

In 1801 Thomas Young shone light through two narrow slits and saw bright and dark stripes on a screen. Where wave crests from both slits meet, they add (bright). Where a crest meets a trough, they cancel (dark). This is interference, the fingerprint of waves. It convinced physicists that light is a wave.

Fire bullets through two slits and you get two heaps behind the slits. Each bullet takes one path, and the heaps simply add. No stripes.

So the test is simple: stripes mean wave, two heaps mean particles.

Now fire electrons, so rarely that only one is in the machine at a time. Each makes a single dot on the screen, like a particle. But after thousands of dots the stripes appear!

One electron cannot have been interfering with a neighbour. Each one seems to have gone through both slits as a wave and landed as a single dot.

cards.h: Watch which slit, and the stripes vanish
cards.b:
Place a detector at the slits to see which one each electron uses. You find each goes through exactly one slit. But now the stripes disappear and you get two heaps.

Finding the path destroys the interference. This is not clumsiness of the detector alone; any way of learning the path, even in principle, kills the stripes. Information is what matters.

cards.h: What is known and what is interpretation
cards.b:
Known (every interpretation agrees)

The probability of landing at a spot comes from adding two amplitudes (the wavefunction contributions of each path). Stripes arise when the paths are not recorded.

Interpretation

What the electron "really did": went through both (Copenhagen-style wave talk), split into many worlds, or followed a guided path (Bohm). Same predictions, different stories.

Analogy breaks: the electron is not a splitting blob. You never see half an electron.

• Young, 1801: light stripes.
  • Davisson-Germer, Thomson, 1927: electron diffraction.
  • Claus Joensson, 1961: electrons through real slits.
  • Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi (Bologna, 1974) and Akira Tonomura's team at Hitachi (1989): single electrons building stripes dot by dot.
  • Arndt, Zeilinger and colleagues, 1999: stripes with C60 molecules; 2019: molecules of over 25,000 atomic mass units (Fein et al., Vienna and Basel).

• "The electron is aware of being watched by a conscious mind." No. Any physical record, even by a mindless atom, destroys the stripes.
  • "The electron splits in two." It always lands whole.
  • "Quantum eraser sends messages to the past." Erasing path information restores stripes only when the data is sorted afterwards. No signal goes backwards.

Urbasi Sinha's group at the Raman Research Institute, Bengaluru, runs single-photon interference experiments. In 2010, with colleagues at Waterloo, she reported a triple-slit test of the rule that probabilities come from adding two-path contributions only (published in Science), finding no sign of extra terms. Such tests also support India's National Quantum Mission aims in photonics.

S.N. Bose's photon counting (1924) is part of the same story: photons that are indistinguishable behave in ways ordinary balls cannot.

• Single electrons land as dots but make stripes in the long run.
  • Learning the path destroys the stripes.
  • The maths is agreed; the story of what happened in between is debated.

Think about it

  1. Why does the stripe pattern build up from single dots prove the stripes are not caused by electrons bumping each other?
  2. What would you expect if a slit were blocked after the electron passed it?

quiz.q: Electrons fired one at a time eventually make:
o: A uniform blur from the start

quiz.q: What happens when you detect which slit each electron used?
Why is the single-electron stripe result surprising?
o: Each electron seems to interfere with itself
quiz.w: It cannot be due to electron-electron collisions.
Showing quantum behaviour in big molecules.

quiz.q: Does consciousness cause the stripes to vanish?
quiz.w: Information in the environment is enough.

quiz.q: Which view says the electron is guided by a pilot wave?
What do all interpretations agree on?
o: The predicted pattern of landing spots
quiz.w: They differ only on the story.
